We just took a brief break for a phone call. And I just asked you, is there anything else you'd like to share about Wilton Cancer School? Well, the only thing was that it really was, it wasn't perfect. I mean, we had problems. We didn't do everything perfect. You know, there were lots of things that I'd do differently. But remember, we were an experimental school. We were trying new ideas. We were trying new things. And that's what Minnesota's lost. We don't have a school like Wilton now, public school, supported by the state, by the college, to experiment, to try new ideas, to do research, do innovation, to do new evaluation techniques, to pioneer, you know, so to speak, to be the NASA, you know, Space Center, the astronauts, you know, of the school. And if we don't have that kind of program, then we, in the state, how are we ever going to progress? Things are going to stay the same, like to stay the same, stay the same. Like, I went to high school with period 1, 2, 3. What's going on in Minnesota today? Period 1, 2, 3, you know. I went to high school like 200 years ago. So when I was in elementary school, you know, grade 1, grade 2, grade 3, what's going on? Grade 1, grade 2, grade 3. Is that the best way for all kids? Maybe it's a good way for some kids, see. Is that the best way for all kids to learn? Is that the best way for all teachers to learn? Does it really bring out the maximum in their teaching ability? Or, and so what we need in the state, and I'd like to see Minnesota State, you know, start it again, is to offer a teacher ed program that would be based on the teacher ed programs that we had at Wilson, but then find schools out around the state. They start with some of the alternative schools as an example. Where they could go out and learn to be a guide by the side instead of the stage by the stage, on the stage. They could also then, a place that could experiment in. So Minnesota State really ought to have, if not one lab school, several schools that they designate as collaborative lab school, right, where the school would be willing to try some things. Then they wouldn't do it with a whole wilted package. But they might try non-grading or non-scheduling or test differently. They're doing, they try new things. And right now we don't have people trying new things. They're just, and even the new legislation about requiring all this reading kind of instruction and all that kind of stuff, you know, it's wrong. Because an article in the Tribune Sunday said that we've got to have these kids catch up because they're behind before they start. How can you be behind if you haven't started? But they've got this idea that you've got to read in kindergarten. And if you're not ready to read in kindergarten, then you're behind. And if you don't read by the third grade, then your life's ruined. It's all wrong. We know it's wrong. And all the reading research will show that. But it's because they have to fit the kids in to the traditional program. Well, at Wilson, kids had 12 years to learn to read. And they all learned to read. My kids went to Wilson. I want them to learn to read, you know. But there wasn't first grade reading class out of Scott Forsman's textbook, you know. We put all in the basement. And so then what's missing from the Minnesota State right now is the research, experimentation, innovation, challenging new ideas, trying things differently. So when I got in trouble with the legislature and called them ranking links, I had support from the college administration. President Nickerson went to bat for me. He said, well, Don may have used the wrong words, but he's got the right ideas. And we're going to go ahead and do it. I'm supporting them, you see. That's the kind of thing that we have. We don't have that now. And we need that kind of spirit. I guess the easiest example is just to put me to have some programs out there. They're sort of the NASA's of education. We're going to the moon. And everybody's going to have to go. But we have to have somebody finding out if this works, if it makes sense, if the rocket will get us there, you know. You know, it will be a risk a little bit. And does education have to stay the same as it's been for 200 years? In my book I wrote, referred to a book called The Tragedy of Education written in 1913 by Edmund Holmes. For 30 years he was a minister of education in England. And they had a real traditional English program then, you know, by the numbers, you know, you do this, this, and this. And he was enforcing it. He was the guy that had to make sure that everybody was on the same page at the same time, you know, that kind of thing. He said, finally, he said, 1911, he said, I can't take this anymore. He wrote a book, 1911, what should be and what could be. In 1913, what tragedy of education described the current traditional system we have now. And he said, I apologize to all the parents and all the kids and all of the people that I did wrong. I spent the rest of my life trying to make up for what I did because the school system in England in the last 30 years has been all wrong. And I've created a tragedy of education. This is the guy that was into it, you see, until he realized that this wasn't working. And Edmund, Bertrand Russell, a famous philosopher and mathematician, wrote a book in 1926 on education. He said, most of us as parents would like to send our kids to school for learning and socialization and so forth. But we would like to send them to the schools that we have. He's a brilliant philosopher, straight-A person, the top mathematician in the country almost at the time, you see. And Margaret Mead in your history sociology kind of thing, Margaret Mead said, my grandmother wanted me to have a good education, so she kept me out of school. Seven U.S. presidents did not graduate from high school. The Wright brothers did not graduate from high school, yet they revolutionized transportation. They changed the world, didn't have a high school diploma. So, you see, we need the Wright brothers pioneering spirit, so we need that effort to try. We can't recreate Wilson now, it's too late, and we wouldn't do it exactly the same anyway. We didn't have computers at Wilson, remember when I did this thing? We had no cell phones, we had no computers, we had no iPods, or whatever you call them. So, now I think what Wilson might be like, but as it turns out, we were the first school in the state to have a computer. It looked like a little freedom, what do you call those boxes? A freedom, adding machine kind of thing. It was kind of a little square box. Because in those days, the university finally got a computer, and they're $100,000 in those days, and you had to have two classrooms in size to house them, and they had the air conditioning. So, obviously, not many people could afford them. Well, man, Kayla finally got one. We didn't get one at Wilson School, but we had a terminal hookup. Okay. So, and our kids could, see, we taught typing in the first grade, too, just like that. We had typewriters, and one of the things in the tape you see on there is that we, one of the kids says, I don't think I'll take typewriters anymore, I'm going to, I'm going to try that computer, you know, this great kid, you know, and, but we had this terminal, and so we, and then we got five other schools tying into this eventually. So, there were six of us in the state that pioneered how to use a computer at the school. It was just like a little free-dating machine. Okay. So, but, you know, that's, that's the kind of spirit we had. It was, it's something new coming along, let's try it, let's give it a whirl. How do you look, this thing called a computer, into a school, you know? Mm-hmm. And so, anyway, that's all I would say. I've got to go over and see Dr. [PERSONA_6], but that's kind of the, you know, I appreciate your interest in knowing more of the history of this thing, and it was a great program. I know times are different now. The world's different. On the other hand, education is still the same. It's the same old schooling. Mm-hmm. And what we need to do is get learning back in the forefront, and we need to get, overcome the politician decisions, and the learning specialist makes the decisions about, you know, kids and learning and so forth, and that's the next step. And if Minnesota State did anything that I'd like to see them do, we'd work out a way to have a pioneering experimentation, research, innovation, accountability kinds of programs, working with some of the schools in the area, and with a Duke teacher ed program, and the, like when I did the teacher ed program here, the kids could still take, the students could still take the traditional teacher program.
